Whanaketia report.
Our solidarity remains with all survivors, past and present, who shared
their stories in hopes of action that we are still waiting to be delivered today.
Mm. Manaaki Rangatahi is a national collective of youth housing advocates who aim
to prevent and end youth homelessness in Aotearoa.
Through our collectives in Kaikohe, Whangārei, Tāmaki Makaurau,
Waikato, Hawke's Bay, Pōneke and Ōtautahi, we work in
collaboration with service providers to ensure rangatahi are housed and have
the necessary wraparound support.
We oppose this bill in its entirety and have concerns particularly
around children experiencing homelessness as young as 14 being targeted.
This is not the first time Māori have been moved on.
Following the signing of Te Tiriti o Waitangi, many tangata whenua have been
displaced from their homes. Whether this was from the violence of land
wars around the country, or more recent history, forcing our
whānau away from their tūrangawaewae to urban centers.
Māori were not homeless peoples. We had abundance in all the
ways you can think of. It wasn't until King Tawhiao
went to negotiate with the Crown in England that he witnessed homelessness for
the first time,
not here in Aotearoa, but in England, where this Parliament's history
begins.
This is a raw reality of being on whenua where horrendous colonial acts of
suppression have taken place and continue to this day.
That is the context that must be remembered as this government aims to move
children on who have nowhere else to go.
Today, this bill continues the colonial legacy of displacement for
tangata whenua and many others who call Aotearoa home.
We thank all the previous submitters highlighting the fact that children are
targeted under this bill.
Our solidarity spans across organizations all around the country, and it is plain
to see that no one wants our children to be on the streets, let alone moved
on.
It's been two years since the Kāinga Kore W2750 report was
released, to which we are claimants of.
Two years of experience and lived experience highlighting the desperate need for
more support, more funding, more care for our homeless whānau.
Yet this government in particular has stripped youth housing providers to bare
bones, changed policy that has resulted in declining people's access to
MSD support and removed emergency housing.
Children do not choose their circumstances.
We recognize our takatāpui LGBTQIA+ rangatahi
who sometimes choose themselves over bigots and are left to fend
for themselves.
We recognize the disabled rangatahi who do not have an accessible house and are
left to sleep wherever they can.
We recognize the rangatahi moving from house to house through Oranga Tamariki.
We recognize rangatahi leaving the criminal justice system with nowhere to go.
At the current age this bill targets, 14-year-olds cannot access
MSD or many housing services because of the strict nature of contracts,
and these are the realities of our young people who are experiencing homelessness
in Aotearoa.
We want to speak to the experience of a young person who is currently in
transitional housing service in Kerikeri-roa.
They were rough sleeping, searching every night for somewhere to sleep,
and they would move to another spot the next day to not
inconvenience anyone.
Those are their words.
Not wanting to be considered an inconvenience.
That is the feelings that they were dealing with while trying to find somewhere
safe, dry place to rest.
They were not harming anyone.
The only harm they experienced was the lack of support for suitable housing that
could support their needs and aspirations.
They're a strong advocate for youth who are homeless, and I thank them for sharing
their story with me to share with you today.
Rangatahi in our collective services are fearful of the police.
It's obvious why when in Kerikeri-roa, an 11-year-old child was
assumed to be an adult mental health patient.
They was then forced into handcuffs and administered antipsychotic
medication
How many more kids are being assumed older by the police?
How many more kids are being targeted by businesses as
nuisances, left to be moved on by police who don't really have the
capacity to deal with our homeless whanau who just want help?
Children often don't have criminal charges before being homeless.
It's the desperation to have a full puku and a good night's
rest that drive them to do things that we wouldn't dream of.
As we state in our submission,
this will create another
pipeline to prison, because when you are desperate, you will do anything to
survive. And that is not an Aotearoa that we should be proud of.
Once you become labeled by the state as a criminal, you cannot get access to many
private and social housing. But everyone deserves a home to go
to. Everyone deserves to be treated like a human being, like every single one of
you.
As this is the Justice Committee, we hope that we can actually see
justice for our children who are rough sleeping and begging throughout Aotearoa.
This bill is spending energy on something that won't work.
Our collective knows the answers to youth homelessness and has been delivering
positive outcomes. This parliament could support the Honorable Marama
Davidson's bill, ensuring that no child is exited out of Oranga Tamariki
without a house and financial support.
It could support or any Kai Parata members bill that will cut to the core of
why our rangatahi are homeless.
We want real solutions to the
catastrophe that is youth homelessness in Aotearoa, and we
actually needed them yesterday. It would have been amazing if these move on
orders were moving people into long-term housing solutions with wraparound support,
but then we wouldn't be here today.
While we cannot trust that this bill will be thrown out, we implore you to do the
bare minimum and raise the age from 14 to 18.
Our children deserve to be treated with dignity and respect.
House our children. Don't criminalize them and push them further into the
margins.
Mm.
Adorn the bird with feathers so that they may fly.
Adorn our rangatahi with housing.
Adorn our rangatahi with an opportunity to thrive so that they can
dream and be the people they want to see in Aotearoa, in this ao.

Yeah. Thanks, Danielle Bianca, for that submission.

to becoming involved with the criminal justice system under this
bill.
Well, the system is incredibly
broken as it currently is. So if you're a rangatahi tonight,
in Aotearoa that's facing housing insecurity and homelessness, you will
find it nearly impossible to find anywhere for yourself.
There isn't front-facing information on how to get
into immediate access or emergency housing.
The system is very complex to navigate.
If you contact MSD, you're going to barely make it to the receptionist,
let alone actually be seen and housed, and you are
advocating for that all by yourself.
So MSD has a system where if you go into MSD, you
then have to go from there to a youth payment provider.
So let's take, for example, MSD Queen Street.
The nearest youth payment provider is Youthline in Epsom.
You have to get there by yourself as a young person, usually with no money,
no HOP card,
no ID, and no way of navigating yourself there.
So how rangatahi fall into the justice system is because
they are falling down all of the gaps that we as Aotearoa are giving to
our rangatahi when they are faced with
houselessness and homelessness.
And we had a rangatahi that we were working with
that was sleeping at the train station in Manukau, and he was going to
join a gang
so that he could get housing and somewhere to sleep.
So if that's not a pipeline into getting involved with
criminal activity and actually
going to somewhere where you know within your own connection and
systems that you can
get some support. If the gangs are the only
place that our rangatahi can go to to get support, we are
incredibly broken as a country. That is just
absolutely abhorrent and our rangatahi deserve better.
And that's not just rangatahi Maori, that's rangatahi that find
themselves on the streets.

your points are well made, and obviously the age is something that people-

Community providers are seeing what's on the ground, and they can

The Wellington City Mission has served the communities of the greater Wellington
region for 122 years now,
and our role is to support those who are struggling the most.
In recent years, this has increasingly been in response to issues of poverty,
a lack of wellbeing, and homelessness.
This makes us, alongside our colleagues and our colleague agencies,
the front line in response to the issues of social and
economic deprivation that have been talked about extensively
throughout your select committee process.
Every day, we see those who are suffering from homelessness, mental
health challenges, addictions, loss of connection with
whānau and friends, and an inability to
obtain and retain
meaningful employment, and many more such issues.
Our lives are interwoven with theirs,
and often we have the honor of being invited into the intimacy of their
lives and their circumstances.
Given that, I want to pose the question that we concluded our written
submission with: What do we do with the
privilege we have?
The privilege that you have,
that I have, that we have. The privilege that so often we take for
granted and assume is available to everyone.
That is not how it is for many people.
So the question today is what are you going to do as members of this committee
with the privilege you have?
Can I commend you on the way you've conducted your hearings over the last two
weeks? I've watched and listened to most of the submissions.
It's not an easy task you have. I don't envy your job.
But I have to acknowledge, throughout it all, you've been generous and
compassionate to every single person you've engaged
with,
irrespective of the views they might have expressed or how they might have
expressed them.
One of our key objectives in the Wellington City Mission is to build a community
where there is no us and them.
What that means in our service delivery is that we treat every
person with dignity and with respect and without
judgment, irrespective of their circumstances.
I believe that you've done that throughout this select committee process.
Thank you.

people in our community that need the most help.
The Wellington City Mission is one of the largest social housing and community
service providers in the Wellington region, and one of the very few that
operates 24/7,
365 days a year.
By definition, therefore, the move on destination for many of the people
who may be impacted by this legislation in Wellington is us.
Let me tell you today that despite our size and capability,
we are full to overflowing.
If we weren't so, there wouldn't be so many people on the streets of Wellington.
Our services are bursting at the seams, as are most of the services of the
community agencies throughout this country.
The myth being postulated by proponents of this bill
is that there's a move on to somewhere better.
But that is in fact a myth.
The Cabinet decision that initiated this legislative proposal was
entitled Strengthening Responses to Public Disorder.
That's a laudable objective and worthy of a government that's acting in the best
interests of
its whole constituency.
The sole issue for us in this proposal is the intention to
extend the powers that are being imposed on the police to
apply to those that aren't contributing to public disorder
but are just trying to survive.

those rough sleeping and begging, he consistently ignores the question
and refers to disorderly behavior in public places and the
need to reclaim our city streets.
None of the minister's commentary justifies why those who are
required to sleep rough and to beg just to survive
are captured by this legal intention.
Unless
maybe we just don't want to see them there.
In considering this bill, you must make the critical distinction
between circumstance
and behaviors.
Behaviors that disrupt, threaten, or offend
should be responded to.

is shame and embarrassment.
Not for them,
but for me,
and for you,
and for all of us. I feel ashamed when some in our community have no legitimate
or safe alternative to sleeping rough.
You should too.
I believe those circumstances to be our failure, not theirs.

Vagrancy Act that criminalized those sleeping rough.

over 3.8 billion pounds over the next three
years.
The country's leadership in the United Kingdom is doing something about this

Our political direction seems to be heading in the other way.

And I don't want to be melodramatic about that, but are we going to be a country

thought we were and aspired to be? If you, as a committee,
recommend to Parliament this bill proceeds into law,
you need to demonstrate the political and moral leadership New Zealand
requires of you. To do that, you need to delete
Section 8
, Subsections E and F. We ask you to please remove
the inclusion of rough sleeping and begging from this bill.

Save the Children was founded in 1919
and has been working in Aotearoa, New Zealand since 1947, and we
focus on advancing the rights of children at all levels, including legislation,
policy, and budgeting for children in order to ensure children's rights are
integral to their daily lives. We welcome the opportunity to share our
submission on the Summary Offences Move on Orders Amendment Bill.
Save the Children does not support the Summary Offences Move on Orders Amendment
Bill.
We agree that disorderly or frightening behavior should be
appropriately addressed, yet we are concerned that the proposed
legislation is targeting some of our most vulnerable citizens and will
criminalize rather than help or address the serious issues of homelessness and
rough sleeping, a lack of income support, and reliance on begging just
to get by. Our concerns related to the proposed amendment
to the legislation include begging, including passive begging, could
become a criminal offense. Rough sleeping could become a
criminal offense. The proposed legislation applies to children
aged 14 to 17 years, and Maori will be
disproportionately affected given they are already
disproportionately affected by homelessness and rough sleeping.
The proposed legislation applies a jail term of up to three months for
breaching a move on order. The legislation moves on or
pushes the serious and complex problems of begging and homelessness out of
sight rather than providing effective solutions, and the
legislation is being rushed through without any consultation of frontline
providers or people already vulnerable who will be most impacted by this
bill.
Ministry of Justice analysis has found that move on orders merely displace
begging behavior and rough sleeping behavior rather than
addressing or resolving it. And this is particularly relevant to
those that are begging, rough sleeping, and creating makeshift dwellings.
These are driven by need. This means that move on orders are highly likely to
shift these behaviors to different locations rather than resolving them,
and are inferior to existing levers for dealing with disorderly behavior
by young people, including referring them to Youth Aid.
The applying of fines for non-compliance with a move on order that was issued for
begging, rough sleeping, or creating a makeshift dwelling are
not effective to these behaviors, and the bill will disproportionately affect
Māori, Pacific, young people, disabled people, and people experiencing
mental health and distress.
Similar to our concerns, we are aware that Auckland councilors have expressed
serious concerns about the bill due to the bill's failure to address the drivers of
rough sleeping and begging, and that the bill will move these behaviors to other
areas, and people lightly become more at risk as they become
separated from support mechanisms that are currently in place to provide help,
such as the Auckland City Mission.
Frontline responders such as Kickback Make Change, Auckland City Mission,
Wellington City Mission, clearly oppose the bill, as do mental health
bodies who are united in their opposition.
So move on. Move on to where? There is nowhere to go.
Living on the street is a symptom of serious social issues and deprivation that
need to be addressed rather than criminalized.
Save the Children's deeply worried that this bill is being introduced at a
time when homelessness and levels of serious deprivation are
increasing.
One in 10 people, or 473,000, are living in
poverty. This means they're unable to afford costs of
rent, power, food, transport, and healthcare, and are making incredibly tough
choices of which one of those they'll be able to pay for.
Youth are particularly affected by youth unemployment, and it's at a 10-year
high. Current welfare and support systems are failing to provide a safety
net for our whānau, our young people, and individuals that need it.
Young people are often invisible in terms of homelessness, as they are unable to
access government supports due to their age, lack the experience and support
mechanisms required to access employment, and are often driven to
homelessness and rough sleeping due to a complete lack of family support networks,
or due to being victims of serious crime and
abuse. According to Statistics New Zealand, in more
than 2023, and we fear it has exacerbated in that time,
112,000 people, or 2.3% of our
population, were estimated to be severely housing deprived.
Children are caught up in severe housing deprivation, and we need to act.
These statistics are particularly grim, and we urge the government to redirect
efforts to meaningfully address these issues by investing in frontline health
and social responses needed to support in response rather than
criminalize, and also to effectively address the drivers of
serious social deprivation that lead to homelessness and begging.
We call on the government to invest in health and social support that will
support and uphold the rights of all of our New Zealanders, including some of our
most vulnerable children, youth, and adults.
It is not acceptable to criminalize those that are most in need of our
help and our compassion. That concludes our submission, and I'm happy to
take any questions.

are their stories? Why do they end up in this situation?

a young person is through experiencing abuse and harm, and sadly,

And we need to be able to address those drivers.
We cannot criminalize these young people who simply have nowhere to go.
We also know that those frontline providers are struggling with funding

And we know from people that reach out and community
stories, and stories feels like the wrong word because it's their

private rental houses is very, very hard, and that is pushing
regular ... well, families that we should be able to house, that are
not beset by addiction and issues, into homelessness.
So it's not limited to people who have addiction
and
those other sort of issues that we sort of see at the frontline of homelessness.

Thank you.
Thank you, Jackie. We don't have any further questions, so thank you very much

Thank you, Kelda.

we're in your hands. Thank you.

love of neighbor, and care for those in need.

DCM in Wellington.

and Murray Edridge touched on this as well.

house or shelter to go to, and they continue to support dozens
of people sleeping rough because there is nowhere else
for them to live.

and social causes.

health, addiction, or multiple challenges at once.

evidence-based support,
not punitive measures. And I'll hand over to

occasion where Jesus of Nazareth was engaged in conversation
and asked a simple question,
"Which command is the greatest?"

would say, smartarsed question, but the jury is out on that,
he is asked, "But who is my neighbor?"

story of the Good Samaritan.

and not in a good way."

in separate locations sitting on the pavement outside the
buildings.

and I felt incredibly humbled.

him, saying my name, getting an enthusiastic, "Kia ora," in
response.

to being called ma'am.
As we parted company, he also graciously wished
